title: NDIS boss calls for a separate watchdog
full_text:
The boss of a top NDIS service provider says a “light touch” appeals process and independent watchdog should be added to the scheme to put guardrails on its automation, as an “AI gold rush” threatens to leave Australians with disabilities behind.
Labor’s sweeping changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme are set pass through parliament next week under an agreement between the government and the Coalition, despite advocates saying the bill “must not pass” without other safety nets in place.
A Senate inquiry into the overhaul will finish on Friday but its recommendations are not expected to make a dent in the legislation, which plans to cut costs by $38bn over four years while removing 241,000 people from the scheme. Automating process claims and decision-making will be central to this reform and Aruma chief executive Martin Laverty told the National Press Club on Monday there was still an opportunity to future-proof the scheme.
During a debate with fellow industry leaders Megan Spindler-Smith and Sophie Cusworth, Dr Laverty said Labor must appoint an independent inspector-general and appeals process to safeguard the scheme’s transformation.
“When have you heard AI referred to in relation to the lives of people with disability where you’ve been able to see some type of benefit derived? At the moment, the AI gold rush is leaving people with disabilities behind,” he said.
“None of us should be particularly concerned about technology being used to undertake administrative tasks – that bit is fine. But please let us have the opportunity to appeal a faulty, incorrect or a dud decision.
“It’s almost un-Australian to be taking away the opportunity to appeal.” Dr Laverty also suggested the sector should continue to pursue reforms while a Labor government was in charge, as opposed to an “uncertain future” under One Nation or the Coalition.
Labor founded the scheme and was best placed to restore the NDIS to its “original intent”, he said.
Concerns have been raised that many participants will no longer be able to appeal over their funding support to an external body under the overhaul, which constrains existing appeal options.
Aruma has suggested Labor should make a replica of the independent taskforce set up by former NDIS minister Bill Shorten in 2019 to clear a backlog of more than 4000 legal appeals.
Resetting incentives, improving the disability employment rate and cracking down on “substandard” behavioural specialists in system were also on the table. Health Minister Mark Butler earlier this year announced sweeping changes to the NDIS after the number of people on the scheme ballooned to 775,000, almost double the initial estimate. Children with mild to moderate autism will be moved off the scheme on to the new Thriving Kids program as Mr Butler declared there was a “life before the NDIS”.
State and territory governments have pushed back against the changes under the state-by-state funding model, which was designed to prevent another “NDIS-lite”. Ms Spindler-Smith, the acting chief executive for Disabilities Australia, said aside from Thriving Kids, there were “still no details” on the support available to adults who would be moved off the scheme.
